question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer: No. When a permanent phases in, rule 702.26d explicitly states that "zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out." Phasing is not actually a change of zones — the permanent never leaves the battlefield, it's just treated as though it doesn't exist while phased out (rule 702.26d), and when it phases back in, its status simply changes to "phased in" and the game again treats it as though it exists (rule 702.26c). Since the permanent never truly left the battlefield, there is no leaves-the-battlefield or enters-the-battlefield event to trigger "when this creature enters" abilities (which are zone-change triggers per rule 603.6a). Additionally, effects that check a phased-in permanent's history won't treat the phasing event as having caused it to leave or enter the battlefield (rule 702.26d), so any "enters the battlefield" abilities that would otherwise care about the timing of entry are unaffected. Similarly, attach/unattach triggers (like an Aura's) also don't trigger from phasing per rule 702.26j, reinforcing that phasing is treated as a non-event for zone- and attachment-based triggers.

Zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Tokens continue to exist on the battlefield while phased out. Counters and stickers remain on a permanent while it’s phased out. Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
A creature with both trample and deathtouch only needs to assign 1 point of combat damage to each blocking creature to satisfy the "lethal damage" requirement for trample, and can then assign all the rest of its damage to whatever it's attacking (a player, planeswalker, or battle).

Here's why: rule [702.19b] says that when an attacking creature with trample is blocked, its controller must assign at least lethal damage to each blocking creature before any excess damage can go through to the defending player/planeswalker/battle, taking into account damage already marked on the blocker and damage from other sources assigned in the same combat damage step. Normally "lethal damage" means enough to reduce the creature's toughness to 0 (accounting for existing marked damage). But rule [702.2c] specifically says: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt." Rule [120.4a] confirms the same principle for damage-replacement effects: any amount of damage greater than 1 is treated as excess damage if the source has deathtouch.

So if, for example, a 6/6 creature with trample and deathtouch is blocked by a 4/4 creature, its controller only has to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 blocking creature to count as "lethal," and can send the remaining 5 damage through to the defending player (or planeswalker/battle it's attacking). That single point of damage will still destroy the blocking creature as a state-based action, since rule [702.2b] and rule [704.5h] both state that any creature with toughness greater than 0 that has been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last state-based action check is destroyed, regardless of how much damage that actually is.

If the attacker also has trample over planeswalkers and is attacking a planeswalker, rule [702.19c] applies: because of deathtouch, 1 damage per blocker still counts as lethal, and after that the attacker only needs to assign damage equal to the planeswalker's loyalty (again, with deathtouch's "any nonzero amount is lethal" rule not applying to planeswalkers directly, since 702.2c only talks about creatures) before excess can go to the planeswalker's controller.

If there are no blocking creatures present when damage is actually assigned (e.g., they were removed from combat), rule [702.19d] says the trampling creature's damage is assigned as though all blockers had been dealt lethal damage — deathtouch doesn't change this, it's already the default case for an unblocked-by-creatures trampler.

One assumption: I'm treating "trample" here as ordinary trample (not just trample over planeswalkers) attacking a creature-blocked combat, which is the standard case the question seems to describe. If the attacker is unblocked entirely, trample's damage-assignment rules don't even come into play per rule [702.19a], since trample only modifies assignment when the creature is blocked.

When checking for assigned lethal damage, take into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other creatures that’s being assigned during the same combat damage step, but not any abilities or effects that might change the amount of damage that’s actually dealt. question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer:
Yes. Storm is a triggered ability that triggers when you cast the spell with storm, and like other triggered abilities it goes on the stack as a non-spell object [603.1a, 702.40a, Storm]. Under rule [113.9], triggered abilities on the stack are not spells, so they can't be countered by effects that only counter spells (like a plain "counter target spell"), but they CAN be countered by effects that specifically say they counter abilities. So a storm trigger is countered only by ability-countering effects (e.g., something like a Ward-style ability that counters abilities, per [Ward]), not by ordinary spell counters.

If the storm trigger itself is countered before it resolves, the copying effect never happens — the original spell that has storm is unaffected and still resolves normally, since the trigger and the spell are separate objects on the stack (the spell is a spell [113.6g], the storm trigger is a triggered ability [603.1a], and each can be dealt with independently).

Note: if a card has multiple instances of storm, each instance triggers and can be countered separately [702.40b].

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer:
No — a hybrid mana symbol counts as ALL of its component colors for deck-legality purposes, not just the color you'd choose to pay it with. Under rule [202.2d], "An object with one or more hybrid mana symbols ... in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols." Rule [107.4e] confirms this directly: "A hybrid mana symbol is also a colored mana symbol, even if one of its components is colorless... A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors." So a card with, say, {R/G} in its mana cost or rules text is both red AND green for color-identity purposes, per [903.4] and [903.4f].

Commander deckbuilding rule [903.5c] (using Wort, the Raidmother as its worked example) requires that every color in a card's color identity also be found in the commander's color identity. Since a hybrid symbol contributes BOTH of its colors to that card's color identity, you can only include such a card if the commander's color identity contains every one of those colors — not just one of them. If your commander is mono-red, for example, a card with an {R/G} hybrid symbol is illegal for that deck, even though you could physically pay that cost entirely with red mana; the fact that you *could* pay with red doesn't change that the card's color identity includes green too.

This is separate from how you actually pay a hybrid cost during the game (you pick one half per [107.4e]/[106.8]/[118.7e]) — that payment flexibility has no bearing on deck construction legality, which is governed purely by color identity as defined in [903.4].

One assumption: I'm treating "only has one of those colors" as meaning the commander's color identity contains one but not all of the hybrid symbol's component colors, which is the case where the card becomes illegal.

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer:
No. You cannot cast spells, activate abilities, or otherwise "respond" to anything during the untap step, because no player receives priority during that step at all. Rule [502.4] states plainly: "No player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast or resolve and no abilities can be activated or resolve." This is reinforced by [117.3a], which says the active player normally gets priority at the start of most steps, but explicitly carves out an exception: "No player receives priority during the untap step."

Within the untap step, the game performs a fixed sequence of turn-based actions with no windows for player interaction in between: first, phased-in permanents the active player controls phase out and previously phased-out ones phase in ([502.1], [703.4a]); second, if the game has a day/night designation, it checks whether that designation should change ([502.2], [703.4b], [731.2]); third, the active player determines and simultaneously untaps the permanents they control ([502.3], [703.4c]). None of these turn-based actions use the stack, so there's nothing to respond to even in principle. Rule [500.3] confirms the untap step is one of the few steps that simply ends once all its specified actions are completed, without any priority ever being passed, and [500.12] confirms no game events can occur in the gaps between steps either.

If something triggers during the untap step (for example, an ability that triggers on a permanent phasing in or out), you still can't respond to it right then — per [502.4], such a trigger is held and doesn't go on the stack until the next time a player would actually receive priority, which is normally the upkeep step. Once the upkeep step begins, the active player gets priority, and any abilities that triggered during the untap step (plus any that trigger at the beginning of upkeep) are put on the stack first, in any order, before that priority is given ([503.1], [503.1a]). At that point, and only at that point, players can respond.

So the practical takeaway: hold your instant-speed responses until the upkeep step (or later), since the untap step itself is a closed sequence of automatic, non-stack-using actions.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer:
Yes. A creature remains an attacking creature until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first — and the combat phase does not end until the end of combat step ends. Since the end of combat step is itself part of the combat phase, attacking creatures are still considered attacking creatures throughout that step; they only stop being attacking creatures (and are formally removed from combat) the instant the end of combat step ends, at which point the combat phase is over and the postcombat main phase begins.

A creature could also stop being an attacking creature earlier, during the end of combat step itself, if something removes it from combat before the step ends — for example, it leaves the battlefield, changes controllers, phases out, stops being a creature, or an effect specifically removes it from combat.

question: Do you cast lands?
answer:
No. A land card is never cast as a spell — it's put onto the battlefield through the special action of "playing" a land, which doesn't use the stack [305.1][701.18a][116.2a]. This is true even for lands that have no mana cost to pay in the first place [202.1b], and even for objects that combine the land type with another card type (like an artifact land): if an object is both a land and another card type, it can still only be played as a land, never cast as a spell [305.9][300.2a][Artifact Land]. Casting is a term reserved for spells going on the stack [601.1][601.1a], and "playing a card" is defined as either playing it as a land or casting it as a spell, whichever is appropriate for that card [701.18b][601.1a] — for a land, that's always "playing," not "casting."

Some mechanical details on playing a land, since the question may really be about how lands enter the battlefield: a player may play a land only during a main phase of their own turn, only while they have priority, only when the stack is empty, and normally only once per turn unless an effect increases that number [305.1][505.6b][116.2a][305.2][305.2b][305.3]. Because it's a special action rather than a spell or ability, it can't be responded to and can't be countered [305.1][505.6b][116.1][117.1]. Note also that effects which "put" a land onto the battlefield (rather than letting a player "play" it) are different from playing a land and don't use up your one-land-per-turn allowance [305.4].

question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer:
Yes. The evoke ability creates a triggered ability ("When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it") that goes on the stack when it triggers, just like any other triggered ability [702.74a]. That sacrifice is part of the ability's *effect*, not a cost paid on entry, so it doesn't happen the instant the creature enters — it only happens when that triggered ability actually resolves. Between the time it triggers and the time it resolves, players get priority and can respond, so if you have some other way to sacrifice the creature (an activated ability, another spell's effect, etc.), you can sacrifice it before the evoke trigger resolves.

If you do sacrifice the creature early this way, then when the evoke triggered ability finally resolves it has nothing left to sacrifice — the creature it was supposed to affect is no longer on the battlefield, so that part of the resolution simply does nothing (you don't get to sacrifice it "again," and no other effect fires off of that non-event). Note this is a separate act of sacrificing: the rule that a single sacrifice can't pay for two different costs or satisfy two different effects [118.10] means the early sacrifice satisfies whatever ability you used it for, not the evoke trigger, and the evoke trigger's own instruction simply fizzles because its object is gone.

Assumption: I'm assuming you have some other legal way to sacrifice the creature (e.g., a sacrifice-outlet ability) that you can use at instant speed after the evoke trigger goes on the stack but before it resolves — evoke itself gives you no way to sacrifice the creature "early," since its own sacrifice instruction is tied to that triggered ability resolving.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. A keyword ability (such as flying, trample, deathtouch, etc.) is simply a shorthand name for an ability whose full rules text is defined elsewhere in the rules — per rule 702.1, "the object lists only the name of the ability as a 'keyword'; sometimes reminder text summarizes the game rule," and rule 702.1d confirms that being described as having a keyword ability is the same as having "a [keyword ability] ability." So keyword abilities are abilities in every rules sense, and an effect that causes a card to lose all abilities removes them along with any other granted or printed abilities.

Rule 113.10 states that an effect removing an ability makes the object lose it, and effects that remove abilities "remove all instances of it" (113.10b) — this applies to every ability the object has, keyword or otherwise, without exception. Rule 603.6d gives a worked example directly on point: if an effect reads "All creatures lose all abilities" and a creature with an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability enters the battlefield, that creature loses its abilities the instant it enters, so its triggered ability (a non-keyword example, but the same removal mechanism) never even triggers. The same removal mechanism strips keyword abilities just as thoroughly.

One caveat: characteristic-defining abilities (rule 604.3) convey information that would normally be found in an object's mana cost, type line, or power/toughness box (e.g., "Changeling" as a CDA context, or something like "Ability X's power/toughness is equal to..."). These are still abilities, so a blanket "loses all abilities" effect removes them too, but doing so can have knock-on effects on the object's other characteristics since the CDA was defining part of them. That's a secondary wrinkle beyond simple keywords like flying or reach, which just vanish outright.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. Maximum hand size only affects the cleanup step, not your ability to draw cards. There is no rule that prevents you from drawing a card just because your hand is already at (or above) your maximum hand size. You can draw normally throughout the turn, ending up with more cards than your maximum hand size if you want.

The restriction only kicks in later: as a turn-based action taken immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven, though a vanguard card's hand modifier can change this, e.g. to six), that player discards down to that number. This is a state-based-action-like turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, and it only applies to the active player's cleanup step — it doesn't stop draws from happening earlier in the turn, and it doesn't apply to non-active players' hands at that point in time.

So you can freely draw cards (from your own effects, opponents' effects, triggered abilities, etc.) even while already at or above your maximum hand size; you'll just need to discard down to your maximum during your own cleanup step if you're still over at that point.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer:
No. In Magic's rules, the term "dies" is a defined technical term that applies only to creatures and planeswalkers — a creature or planeswalker "dies" if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield ([Dies], [700.4]). A non-creature artifact is neither a creature nor a planeswalker, so when it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield (whether by being destroyed, sacrificed, or otherwise), that event is not called "dying" in the rules sense — it's just being put into the graveyard.

Note the exception: if an artifact is also a creature (an "artifact creature"), it combines the aspects of both types ([300.2]), and since it is a creature, it does die when put into a graveyard from the battlefield. So the distinction is really about creature status, not about being an artifact — a plain (non-creature) artifact never dies, but an artifact creature does.

This matters for triggered abilities worded "whenever a creature dies" — those won't trigger off a non-creature artifact going to the graveyard, only off creatures (including artifact creatures) doing so.

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You don't lose the game instantly at the moment of the failed draw — instead you attempt the draw, get nothing (since there's no card to put into your hand), and then you lose the game the next time any player would receive priority, because the empty-library draw attempt is checked as a state-based action.

Mechanically: drawing a card means moving the top card of your library into your hand [121.1]. If your library has zero cards, that's impossible, so as much of the action as can happen does (in this case, nothing) [609.3]. The fact that you attempted to draw from an empty library is then caught by the state-based action rule: 'If a player attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it since the last time state-based actions were checked, that player loses the game' [704.5b]. This is echoed in [121.4] and [104.3c], both of which say the player loses the game the next time a player would receive priority (state-based actions are checked continuously right before priority would be given, per [704.1]).

A related wrinkle: if you're required to draw *more* cards than remain in your library (e.g., you have 2 cards left but must draw 3), you draw the remaining cards you can and then lose under the same rule [104.3c]. And even with an empty library, any effect that replaces a draw (rather than a plain draw) still applies — it isn't skipped just because there was nothing to draw [121.6a], [614.11].

One assumption: I'm treating 'should draw a card' as an actual attempted draw (turn-based action in your draw step, or an effect telling you to draw) rather than an optional 'may draw' effect. If it's an optional draw and your library is empty, you're still allowed to choose to draw [121.3], and doing so would trigger the same empty-library loss condition once resolved.

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
The combat phase has five steps, in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped entirely if no creatures are attacking [506.1], and there are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1].

As the defending player, you get priority in each step only after any required turn-based actions for that step are completed, and after the active player has had priority and passed it to you. Turn-based actions don't use the stack and happen automatically without anyone needing priority: for example, you as the defending player perform the turn-based action of declaring blockers at the start of the declare blockers step [509.1] [703.4j], and combat damage assignment and dealing are also turn-based actions that occur before any priority is passed in the combat damage step [510.1] [703.4k] [510.2] (no player may cast spells or activate abilities between damage being assigned and dealt [510.2]). Only after these turn-based actions are done does the normal priority system kick in, per the general priority rule that a player with priority may cast spells or activate abilities [117.1].

The one step where the rules explicitly confirm who gets priority first is the end of combat step: once it begins, the active player gets priority first [511.1], meaning you as the defending player receive priority only after the active player passes. I'm assuming (since the provided rules don't spell this out for every step) that the same active-player-first pattern holds for beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, and combat damage as well, based on the normal turn structure — if that assumption is wrong for some specific step, the practical effect would be that you might get first priority in that step instead, but nothing in the provided rules suggests that.

This answer holds the same whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game, except that in multiplayer games without an 'attack multiple players' or similar option, there's also a turn-based action where the active player chooses which opponent becomes the defending player at the very start of the beginning of combat step [506.2a] [507.1] [703.4h]; in multiplayer variants where all opponents automatically become defending players (like the Attack Multiple Players option), that choice step is skipped [802.2].

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer:
No. Paying a cost isn't itself a stack action, so there's no window where other players get priority to respond specifically to the moment a cost is paid.

A cost is just "an action or payment necessary to take another action" [118.1]. Costs get paid in a few different contexts, and none of them give opponents a chance to respond in between:

- When casting a spell or activating an activated ability, the costs (mana, additional costs, etc.) are paid as part of the casting/activation process itself, before the spell or ability is ever put on the stack [602.1, 118.2]. Since the spell/ability isn't on the stack yet during that process, no one can respond to it, and nothing can be inserted to respond to just the cost-paying step.
- If mana is needed to pay a cost, the paying player gets a chance to activate mana abilities to generate that mana [118.2]. But mana abilities don't use the stack [605.1], so there's nothing there to respond to either.
- During combat, declaring attackers or blockers (which can involve paying costs) is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [508.1j, 509.1e, 509.1f]. Again, no stack step exists for anyone to respond to.
- Some abilities phrase part of their effect as a cost paid on resolution, e.g. "[Do something]. If you do, [effect]" — that cost is paid during the resolution of the already-stacked ability [118.12]. At that point the ability is already resolving, so there's no separate opportunity to respond to just the cost-payment sub-step; you could only have responded earlier, while the ability was still on the stack before it started resolving.

So in every case, the earliest thing you could actually respond to (with priority) is the spell or ability itself once it's on the stack — not the act of paying its cost. If a cost can't be paid at all (because it's illegal, unpayable, or the player can't complete it), the whole attempted action is undone under rule 733.1, but that's a rules-legality check, not something you "respond" to with your own spells or abilities.

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
The layer system is the set of rules that determines the order in which continuous effects are applied to figure out an object's current characteristics (power, toughness, color, types, abilities, etc.) [Layer]. This matters because multiple effects can be trying to change the same object at once, and the order they're applied in can change the result.

Here's how it works, per rule [613.1]: you start with the object's actual/printed characteristics (or, for a token or copy, the characteristics defined by the effect that made it), and then apply every applicable continuous effect in a fixed sequence of layers:

- Layer 1: Rules/effects that modify copiable values [613.1a], split into sublayers (1a is copy effects) [613.2], [613.2a]
- Layer 3: Text-changing effects [613.1c], [612.1]
- Layer 4: Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d]
- Layer 5: Color-changing effects [613.1e]
- (Layer 6, not shown in the provided rules, covers ability-adding/removing effects, per the Act of Treason example in [613.6])
- Layer 7: Power/toughness effects, itself split into sublayers (7a setting base P/T by characteristic-defining abilities, 7b other P/T-setting effects, 7c P/T-modifying effects like +1/+1 or counters), applied in that sublayer order [613.4]

Every effect is slotted into whichever layer matches what it actually does — an effect can even span multiple layers if it does more than one kind of thing. For example, "This creature gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice" has its color-changing part applied in layer 5 and its +1/+1 part applied in layer 7c [613.6]. If an effect starts modifying a set of objects, it keeps applying to that same set in each relevant layer even if the source of the effect later disappears [613.6].

Within a single layer (or sublayer), if more than one effect applies, you order them by timestamp — the effect that started applying earlier goes first [613.7]. However, if a dependency exists between effects in that same layer/sublayer (one effect's outcome literally depends on whether/how another effect applied), the dependency system overrides the timestamp order [613.8].

All of this happens continuously and automatically as the game state changes — there's no need for anyone to manually recalculate; characteristics are always current [613.5]. The classic illustration: Honor of the Pure gives "white creatures you control +1/+1." If a black 2/2 creature is turned white by a layer 5 effect, it now qualifies and gets +1/+1 in layer 7c, becoming 3/3; if its color is later changed to red, Honor of the Pure stops applying and it reverts to 2/2 [613.5].

Note: the rules I have don't include the actual text of layer 2 (control-changing effects) or layer 6 (ability-adding/removing effects) themselves — only the general structure rule [613.1] and examples referencing them via [613.6]. The layer order overall runs 1 through 7 as listed above, with 2 and 6 fitting between the ones I can quote directly.

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
The legend rule is a state-based action that prevents a player from controlling two or more legendary permanents with the same name at once. If a single player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the same name, that player must choose one of them to keep, and all the others are put into their owners' graveyards [Legend Rule] [704.5j].

Key details:
- It only applies to legendary permanents controlled by the SAME player. If two different players each control a legendary permanent with the same name, the legend rule doesn't apply to either of them, since each player individually controls only one copy [704.5j].
- Any permanent with the supertype "legendary" is subject to this rule [205.4d].
- Legendary planeswalkers are included too. Older planeswalkers were once restricted by a separate "planeswalker uniqueness rule" based on planeswalker type, but that's been removed; those cards now have the legendary supertype and are checked under the ordinary legend rule instead, just like any other legendary permanent [306.4].
- Because it's a state-based action, it's checked automatically whenever a player would receive priority, not something anyone has to remember to activate manually.
- The comparison is strictly by name. Two legendary permanents only trigger the rule if their names are identical; having the same card type, subtype, or supertype isn't enough on its own.
- Note this rule only concerns legendary permanents (things on the battlefield). A separate, unrelated restriction exists for legendary instants/sorceries: those can't even be cast unless the caster controls a legendary creature or legendary planeswalker [205.4e], but that's a casting restriction, not the legend rule itself.

So in short: same player, same name, legendary permanents → keep one, the rest go to their owners' graveyards.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature doesn't die the instant damage is marked on it — it dies as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked, which happens automatically before any player would next receive priority.

Here's the sequence: when a source deals damage to a creature, that damage is marked on it [120.3e][302.7]. Damage itself never destroys the creature — rather, once the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, it "has been dealt lethal damage" and becomes eligible to be destroyed by a state-based action [120.5][120.6][Lethal Damage]. State-based actions are checked continuously: every time a player would receive priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions, and repeats until none remain, before that player actually gets priority [117.5][704.1]. So in practice, if your creature takes lethal damage during, say, the combat damage step, it will be destroyed essentially immediately afterward — before either player gets a chance to act — because the game checks state-based actions before doling out priority [704.5g].

One nuance: damage marked on a creature persists across the rest of the turn (it isn't removed until the cleanup step) [120.6][514.2], so a creature can also end up destroyed later in the turn if additional damage (or a toughness reduction) pushes cumulative marked damage to lethal, again via a state-based action the next time one is checked. If nothing intervenes, that check happens right after the damage event, so functionally your creature dies right away.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
Generally no — a commander sitting in exile can't be cast directly; the game only lets you cast a commander from the command zone. If your commander card is in exile, you (as its owner) may move it to the command zone as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked (this is optional, not automatic), and only then can you cast it from the command zone as described in rule 903.8. So the practical path is: exile → command zone (state-based action) → cast from command zone, paying the commander tax.

Rule [903.8] then says a player may cast a commander they own from the command zone, and that doing so costs an additional {2} for each previous time that player has cast that commander from the command zone that game (the 'commander tax'). Casting in general requires that some rule or effect specifically permit casting the spell from wherever it currently is [601.3f], and nothing in the rules provided gives a generic permission to cast a commander directly out of exile — only out of the command zone.

Exception: if the physical card happens to have its own ability that lets you cast spells from exile with certain qualities (for example, a Plot ability under [702.170d], or an Adventure exile under [715.3d]), that ability's own text overrides the general rule and would let you cast the card from exile under its own terms — that's a property of the card's own text, not of it being your commander. If you don't have such an ability in play, assume you must first send it to the command zone via the state-based action and cast it from there.

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer:
During the cleanup step, three things happen, mostly without any player getting priority. First, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard down to that number [514.1][703.4n]. Second, simultaneously: all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed, and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end [514.2][703.4p][120.6]. Normally no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated [514.3][514.3a]. However, if the discard (when necessary) causes a state-based action to need to be performed, or if any triggered abilities are waiting to go on the stack (including ones that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"), those state-based actions are performed, then those triggers are put on the stack, and the active player gets priority so players can cast spells and activate abilities [514.3a][704.3]. Once the stack is empty and everyone passes in succession, a new cleanup step begins [514.3a]. If nothing like that happens, the step just ends without anyone getting priority [500.3][704.3].

question: when can I concede a game?
answer: You can concede a game at any time — there's no restriction on timing. Rule 104.3a says a player who concedes leaves the game immediately and loses that game, and this can happen at any point during the game, not just during priority windows. This is even true if another player is controlling you (via some effect): rule 723.6 makes clear the controller of another player can't force that player to concede, but the player themselves may still concede whenever they choose. Rule 405.6g also confirms that conceding doesn't use the stack, so it's not something that can be responded to or countered — it just happens the instant you do it. Notably, rule 101.1 singles this out as the one thing card text can never override: even if a card says something like 'a player can't concede,' that would be ignored, since conceding is the sole exception to the 'card text overrides the rules' principle. question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply whoever's turn it is right now. Per rule 102.1, "the active player is the player whose turn it is," and every other player at the table is a nonactive player for that turn.

A few clarifications that can matter in practice:

- This changes only at whoever's turn it becomes — it's not tied to who's attacking, who has priority, or who controls the stack. In fact, the active player is specifically the one who gets priority first in most steps and phases (rules 504.2, 507.2, 508.2, 509.2, 510.3, 505.6), so "who has priority first" is a symptom of being active, not the definition of it.

- If a player is being controlled by another player or effect during their own turn, they are still the active player — only control of that player changes, not whose turn it is (rule 723.3).

- During the combat phase in a two-player game, the active player is specifically called the attacking player, and the single nonactive player is the defending player (rule 506.2). In a multiplayer game where opponents don't automatically all become defending players, the active player picks one opponent to be the defending player (rule 507.1) — this doesn't change who the active player is, just who defends.

- If an ability refers to "the active player" in a context where there could be more than one at once (e.g., certain multiplayer variants), the ability's controller picks which specific active player it means when the effect applies (rule 805.9).

- In games using the shared team turns option, it's a whole team's turn rather than one person's — that team is the "active team," and every other team is a nonactive team (rule 805.4a). Individual "active player" language in that context is adjusted by the team rules (805.6), but you asked about a single active player, so the short answer for a standard (non-team) game stands: check whose turn it currently is.

question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
answer: Yes. If you had priority before you cast a spell, you get priority back immediately after that spell finishes being cast (rule 601.2i: "If the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority."; see also 117.3c). Because of this, you can "hold priority" — instead of passing, you cast another spell (or activate an ability, or take a special action) right away, before anyone else gets a chance to act and before the first spell resolves. Each new spell or ability you cast or activate while you still have priority goes on top of the stack and resolves before the earlier ones, per rule 117.7 ("the new spell or ability will resolve first"). You can chain this as many times as you like — cast spell A, retain priority, cast spell B in response, retain priority, cast spell C in response, and so on — as long as each casting is legal and you had priority beforehand. The same logic applies to activating abilities (117.1) and to taking special actions, which also return priority to the acting player afterward (116.3). Eventually, once you choose to pass priority instead of acting again, the other player(s) get a chance to respond, and the stack only finishes resolving down to empty once all players pass in succession with nothing on it (rule 500.2). question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by a resolving spell or ability (or by a replacement effect being applied, or by a static ability that lets a player take an action) that will do something at a later time rather than immediately. Even though it's created "now," it doesn't trigger right away — instead it sits and waits for its trigger condition, and it will contain the word "when," "whenever," or "at" somewhere in its text (though that word usually isn't the very first word). For example, an effect might say "Exile this creature at the beginning of the next end step" — that's a delayed triggered ability that waits until the next end step to actually exile the permanent. Once its trigger event happens, it goes on the stack like any other triggered ability. A delayed triggered ability normally triggers only once (the next time its trigger event occurs) unless it specifies a duration like "this turn," and it won't trigger at all if it was never actually created before its trigger event already passed, or if the object it refers to has left the zone it's expected to be in by the time it would resolve.
